Defibrillators (AED) & CPR
Do
Do not apply a tight tourniquet, ice, alcohol or an electric shock.
Do not chase or try to kill the snake, and do not wait to “see if it was venomous”.
Do not cut the wound or try to suck out the venom.
Do not dismiss a minor scratch or a lick on broken skin — these can pass on rabies too.
Do not drink the tap water. Bottled and filtered water is cheap and everywhere, with refill stations in most towns. Ice in cafés and restaurants is factory-made and generally safe.
Do not make them stand up or walk around.
Do not rub the area or rinse with fresh water — it can fire more stinging cells.
Do not scrub hard enough to bruise the tissue, and do not have the wound stitched closed straight away unless a doctor decides it is necessary — leave it open after washing.
Do not use urine.
Do not wait for symptoms to worsen before using adrenaline.
Do not wait to “see if the animal was sick”, and do not assume a calm or healthy-looking animal is safe.
Dress modestly at temples (shoulders and knees covered) and more conservatively in rural and Muslim-majority areas; it draws less attention and respects local custom.

For a stonefish or stingray wound, soak the area in water as hot as can be comfortably tolerated (around 45°C). A sea-urchin puncture is different: wash it with soap and water instead — do not use the hot-water method on that one.
Get out of the water. Douse the sting with vinegar for at least 30 seconds — many beaches keep a bottle for this.

Get to a clinic or hospital the same day for rabies post-exposure vaccination — do not wait for symptoms. Dog, cat, monkey and bat bites or scratches across this region can carry rabies, which is almost always fatal once symptoms begin but is nearly always preventable when treatment starts promptly.
Get to a hospital even if they improve — symptoms can return hours later.
Get to a hospital that can give antivenom as fast as possible, and call the emergency number on the way.
Honest guidance on adrenaline auto-injectors and defibrillators — neither is reliably bought on the street in this region — plus hands-only CPR.

Eat where locals queue and food is cooked to order. Be extra careful with ice, salads and shellfish in rural areas and the hot season; peel your own fruit.
In Phnom Penh, bag-snatching from passing motorbikes is the main risk: wear bags across the body on the side away from the road, and keep your phone out of sight near traffic.
Tap water is not safe to drink. Stick to sealed bottled or filtered water and check the seal. Outside the cities, ask for drinks without ice unless you are sure it is commercial ice.
Use Grab or the PassApp for tuk-tuks and cars, so the fare and route are logged.
Do not drink the tap water. Bottled water is widely sold and refill stations exist in tourist towns. Outside the main towns, ask for no ice unless you know it is commercial.
Freshly grilled and boiled dishes from busy stalls are safest. Avoid raw or fermented meat/fish dishes such as laap dib — they carry a real parasite risk. Peel fruit yourself.
Laos is very relaxed and low-crime, but towns wind down early — plan transport before dark, especially in rural areas where lighting and taxis are scarce.
On tubing or river days around Vang Vieng, be careful with alcohol near fast water; this is the main cause of traveller injuries.
Busy stalls with high turnover are safest — choose freshly cooked, steaming dishes. Go easy on raw herbs you cannot wash yourself and on shellfish in hot weather.
Carry bags on the pavement side and keep phones away from the kerb; snatch-thefts from passing motorbikes happen in Ho Chi Minh City and Hanoi.
Do not drink the tap water. Use bottled or filtered water; most hotels supply it free. Café and bia-hơi ice in cities is normally commercial ice and fine.

Road or scooter accident
By far the most likely serious emergency a traveller faces in this region.
Get out of the traffic lane before anything else. Being hit a second time is a real risk on a fast road, and it is what turns a survivable crash into a fatal one.
Call the national emergency number. Say the road, the direction of travel and the nearest landmark or kilometre marker — a screenshot of your map pin is the fastest way to answer "where are you?".
Do not move anyone who has hit their head or complains of neck or back pain, unless leaving them is more dangerous than moving them.
Control heavy bleeding with firm, continuous pressure through whatever cloth you have. Keep pressing; do not lift to check.
Go to hospital even if you feel fine. Head injuries and internal bleeding declare themselves hours later, and road rash here infects fast in the heat.
Get a police report. Without one, most travel insurance and every vehicle claim is disputed. Ask for the report number before you leave.
Photograph everything at the scene: both vehicles, the road, the position, any licence and registration, and the other rider. Photographs settle later arguments that memory cannot.

Tell your insurer the same day. Many policies exclude motorcycle injury unless you hold a licence valid for that engine size and were wearing a helmet — know which before you rent, not after you crash.
Do not hand over your passport as security to a rental shop, a hospital or anyone at the scene. Offer a photocopy or a deposit instead — a withheld passport is the standard lever in a rental dispute.
Do not agree a cash settlement at the roadside before you know the extent of your own injuries.

Drink spiking & methanol poisoning
Rare but not hypothetical — and methanol poisoning is survivable only if it is recognised early.
Treat sudden severe drunkenness that does not match how much was drunk as an emergency, especially after free shots, mixed spirits or home-made liquor.

Methanol poisoning classically appears 6–30 hours after drinking, not immediately: blurred or snowy vision, severe stomach pain, breathlessness, confusion. Any vision change after drinking spirits is a hospital emergency that night, not in the morning.
Get the person to the largest hospital you can reach and say the words "possible methanol poisoning". Treatment exists and works; delay is what kills.
If someone is unconscious but breathing, put them on their side so they cannot choke, and stay with them.
Keep the bottle, the glass or the receipt if you safely can — it helps the hospital and any investigation.
Report it to the tourist police and to your embassy. Clusters are how these venues get shut.
Do not let anyone "sleep it off" alone in a room. Almost every death in a spiking or methanol cluster involves someone left to sleep.
Do not accept drinks from a shared jug or a bucket you did not watch being poured, and do not leave a drink unattended.
Lost or stolen passport
Recoverable, but the order of the steps decides whether it takes two days or two weeks.
Report it to the local police and get a written report with a reference number. Every embassy asks for it, and so does your insurer.
Contact your embassy or consulate — the nearest one is usually in Bangkok, Hanoi, Ho Chi Minh City or Phnom Penh, and many countries have none at all in Laos.
If your visa or entry stamp was in it, immigration will need to reissue the record before you can leave the country. Start that on the same day.
Ask for an emergency travel document if you have a flight soon; a full replacement passport takes longer and may have to be issued from a regional hub.
Cancel and replace any cards that went with it, and change the passwords for anything that was unlocked on a stolen phone.
Do not leave the country by land while the entry record is unresolved — an unmatched entry stamp turns a lost passport into an immigration problem.
Do not rely on the photocopy alone. Keep a photograph of the data page and the entry stamp somewhere you can reach without your phone.

Robbery, theft or assault
Snatch theft from a moving motorbike is the common version, and it injures people because they hold on.
Let it go. A bag is replaceable; being dragged along a road is how snatch theft causes serious injury and death.
If you are hurt, treat that first and go to hospital — the report can be made afterwards.
Report it to the tourist police where there is a tourist police unit; they usually have English speakers and handle traveller cases directly.
Freeze cards immediately and check for transactions — card cloning at ATMs is common in this region.
Get the written police report for your insurer; a verbal report is not enough for a claim.
Tell your embassy if a passport, a visa or your safety is involved.
Do not chase anyone, and do not confront a group.
Do not carry your only card, your only phone and your passport in the same bag.
Arrested or detained
Drug offences carry severe penalties across all four countries, including sentences travellers do not expect.
Ask immediately, clearly and repeatedly to contact your embassy. You are entitled to consular access; the request is what triggers it.
Do not sign anything you cannot read, and say so plainly. Ask for a translated copy and for a lawyer.
Stay calm and polite. Argument and raised voices make everything that follows harder.
The embassy can supply a list of local lawyers, contact your family and monitor your treatment.
Arrange money through family or your insurer rather than through anyone who approaches you at the station.
Do not offer money to a police officer. In a genuine arrest it converts a bad situation into a far worse one.
Do not assume a substance is legal because it is sold openly to tourists — cannabis law in Thailand has changed more than once and differs completely in the other three countries.
In trouble in the water
Drowning is the second leading cause of traveller death here, and rip currents cause most of it.
Caught in a rip: do not swim against it. Float, signal, and swim parallel to the beach until the pull stops, then come in at an angle.
Helping someone else: throw them something that floats and call for help. Swimming out to a panicking person is how one drowning becomes two.
Out of the water and not breathing: start chest compressions immediately — hard and fast in the centre of the chest, about twice a second — and send someone for an ambulance.
Anyone who has been under the water needs hospital assessment even if they seem fine afterwards.

For a jellyfish sting, flood the area with vinegar for at least thirty seconds and treat any breathing difficulty as an emergency. Box jellyfish are present in the Gulf of Thailand and around the Cambodian coast.
Do not swim where a red flag is flying, and do not judge a beach by how calm it looks — rips are strongest where the water appears flattest.
Do not drink and swim, and do not swim alone at night.

High fever
Dengue is the biggest infectious risk to travellers in this region, and it is seasonal rather than rare.
Any fever above 38 °C that lasts more than 24 hours needs a doctor and a blood test. Dengue, malaria and typhoid all start looking like flu.
Take paracetamol for fever and pain — nothing else.
Drink steadily. Dehydration is what turns a manageable dengue into an admission.
Warning signs that mean hospital now, not tomorrow: severe stomach pain, repeated vomiting, bleeding gums or nose, black stools, breathlessness, or a sudden drop in temperature with cold clammy skin.
Malaria is a risk in forested border areas rather than the cities. Tell the doctor exactly where you have been in the last month.
Do not take ibuprofen, aspirin or any other anti-inflammatory until dengue has been ruled out — they increase bleeding risk.
Do not buy antimalarials or antibiotics from a small shop; counterfeit medicine is a genuine problem outside established pharmacies.
Severe stomach illness
Common, usually self-limiting, and occasionally the thing that puts a traveller on a drip.
Rehydrate with oral rehydration salts, sold in every pharmacy in the region. Water alone does not replace what is being lost.

Someone collapses, or will not wake up
Check for a response — speak loudly and gently shake their shoulders (a baby: tap the foot, do not shake).
If they respond and are breathing normally: do not move them if you suspect a neck or back injury; otherwise put them in the recovery position (below) and keep checking their breathing.
If they do NOT respond: shout for help, and check breathing for up to 10 seconds — look, listen, feel. Noisy, gasping or irregular breathing counts as "not breathing normally".

Not breathing, or not breathing normally: call the emergency number on speakerphone (or send someone to) and start CPR immediately — see the adult/child or baby steps below. Do not wait to find a pulse; lay rescuers are not asked to check for one.
Send someone to find an AED (defibrillator) if one might be nearby — large hotels, malls and airports sometimes have one.
CPR — adult and child over about 1 year
Lay them on their back on a firm, flat surface.
Heel of one hand on the centre of the chest (lower half of the breastbone); for a child, one or two hands depending on their size.
Push hard and fast: adult depth 5–6 cm, child about one-third of the chest’s depth (roughly 5 cm) — both at 100–120 pushes per minute, letting the chest fully rise between pushes.

If trained and willing: 30 pushes, then 2 rescue breaths, repeating (children may be given 15:2 if there are two trained rescuers). If untrained, unwilling, or unable to give breaths: continuous push-only CPR is still far better than nothing.
Use an AED the moment one arrives and follow its voice prompts — it will not shock unless a shock is needed.
Keep going until the person starts breathing normally, professional help takes over, or you are physically unable to continue.

Alone with no phone: with an adult, call first, then start CPR. With a child, current guidance is to give CPR for about one to two minutes first if you truly cannot call and compress at the same time (put the phone on speaker and start compressions the moment you have dialled, if that is possible instead).

A rescuer taught with breaths first (5 initial breaths before compressions, still taught in the UK/Europe for children) and one taught compressions-first (the US/AHA approach) are both following a currently-endorsed method — do not hesitate over which to use.
CPR — baby under 1 year
Lay the baby on their back on a firm surface, head in a neutral position (not tilted back).
For rescue breaths, your mouth covers the baby’s mouth AND nose.

Compress the lower half of the breastbone, just below the nipple line, using two thumbs wrapped around the chest (preferred where you can manage it) or the heel of one hand if you cannot encircle the chest — two fingers is also still taught in some countries and is not wrong if that is what you learned.
Push at least one-third of the chest’s depth (about 4 cm), 100–120 per minute.
30 compressions to 2 breaths for a single rescuer; 15:2 if there are two trained rescuers.
Keep going until the baby responds, help takes over, or you cannot continue.

Which hand technique is "correct" is genuinely still shifting between countries as of 2026 — two-thumb encircling is now preferred almost everywhere, but two-finger and heel-of-one-hand are still taught and are not mistakes.

Recognise anaphylaxis (severe allergic reaction)

Sudden breathing or circulation trouble after a food, sting or medicine: swelling of the tongue or throat, noisy or difficult breathing, a wheeze or persistent cough, a hoarse voice, difficulty swallowing, dizziness or collapse.
Often — but not always — with hives or skin swelling. A reaction can be severe with no skin signs at all.
In babies and young children specifically: sudden pale, floppy or limp, not responding normally.
Anaphylaxis — what to do
If an adrenaline (epinephrine) auto-injector is available, use it AT ONCE into the outer mid-thigh — through clothing is fine.
Call the emergency number straight away.
Lie the person flat and raise their legs; if breathing is very hard, let them sit up instead. Someone pregnant should lie on her left side.
Do not let them stand or walk, even once they feel better — a sudden drop in blood pressure while upright can be fatal.
No improvement after about 5 minutes and a second auto-injector is available: give the second dose.
Go to hospital every time, even after a full recovery — symptoms can return hours later (a biphasic reaction).

If in genuine doubt whether it is anaphylaxis, every source agrees: give the adrenaline. The risk of a dose given when it was not strictly needed is far smaller than the risk of withholding it when it was.
Anaphylaxis in babies and children
Lay a baby or toddler flat — never hold them upright.
Use their own prescribed auto-injector at its prescribed dose the moment anaphylaxis is suspected.
Auto-injector doses run roughly: 0.1 mg for about 7.5–15 kg (where that device exists), 0.15 mg from about 7.5–20 kg up to 30 kg depending on country and device, 0.3 mg above about 20–30 kg.
Under about 7.5 kg, or any child with no prescribed device: call the emergency number immediately and let paramedics or a doctor decide the dose — do not improvise with a mismatched adult device.
Dosing bands genuinely differ between countries and auto-injector brands — this is not a single fixed number worldwide. Always follow the child’s own prescribed device and plan where one exists.
Asthma attack
Help them sit upright — never lie them down. Stay calm; anxiety worsens breathing.
Use the blue/grey reliever inhaler at once, with a spacer if one is available.
They have their own written asthma action plan: follow its dosing exactly.

No plan: either recognised approach is safe — 1 puff every 30–60 seconds up to 10 puffs (UK-style), or 4 puffs (one at a time via a spacer, 4 breaths each), wait 4 minutes, then repeat (Australia-style).

Call the emergency number if: there is no inhaler, the inhaler is not helping, lips or fingers turn blue, the person is exhausted or confused, breathing becomes quiet or slow, or symptoms have not resolved after the full first round.
Severe bleeding
Apply firm, continuous direct pressure over the wound with whatever is available — a cloth, clothing, your hand.

Life-threatening limb bleeding not controlled by pressure: apply a tourniquet a few centimetres above the wound — never over a joint — and tighten until the bleeding stops. Note the exact time it went on and do not loosen it.
A deep wound somewhere a tourniquet cannot go (neck, groin, armpit): pack the wound firmly and press.

A lightning-strike victim carries no electrical charge — it is safe to touch them immediately and start CPR if they are not breathing.
Calling for help in Thailand — beyond the main number

1669 (medical emergency/ambulance) is free from any phone, works nationwide 24 hours, and operators can usually handle basic English — say "English" as soon as the call connects. Response is markedly slower on islands and in rural areas than in Bangkok.
191 is police, 199 is fire — both free and 24 hours.
1155 is the Tourist Police: a free, 24-hour hotline specifically staffed for English-speaking travellers — a good parallel or backup call, though not a replacement for 1669 in a medical emergency.
1367 is the Ramathibodi Poison Center’s 24/7 consultation hotline.
1199 is the Marine Department’s 24-hour hotline for water incidents (boats, ferries, accidents at sea).
This is Thailand-specific detail underneath the country’s own main emergency number, which this app already shows at the top of the SOS and hospital screens for whichever country you are in.
Insurance and getting evacuated
Comprehensive travel insurance covering medical treatment AND emergency evacuation (including from remote islands) is not optional here — do not assume your home healthcare system covers this.
Foreigners are charged for all medical treatment; there is no reciprocal free-healthcare arrangement.

Private hospitals — the fastest, highest-standard option — commonly want a deposit or a formal insurer "guarantee of payment" before non-emergency treatment. Even with insurance, you may be billed as self-pay until that guarantee arrives, which can take 24–72 hours or more.
Call your insurer’s assistance line as early as possible — ideally before admission, not after.
Malaria, dengue and Japanese encephalitis risk

Malaria in Thailand is concentrated in remote, forested border areas (with Cambodia, Myanmar and Malaysia) — the tourist islands themselves are low or negligible risk, and routine antimalarial tablets are generally not needed for an island or beach trip.

Dengue is different: it is endemic across Thailand, Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos, including all the islands, year-round with a rainy-season peak. There is no vaccine relied on for casual travel — bite avoidance (repellent, covering clothing, screens) is the real prevention.

Japanese encephalitis occurs countrywide outside Bangkok, peaking seasonally (roughly May–October), and is weighted toward rural, rice-farming areas. Vaccination is mainly advised for longer stays (a month or more) or higher-risk itineraries.
Anyone trekking into remote forest near an international border should get individual pre-trip travel-clinic advice regardless of the above.
